claims.text: The 12-13 November 2026 Microsoft 365 outage was widely covered, with restored servers becoming unresponsive under traffic
Retries amplify load, and backoff with jitter plus retry limits help
Retries and queued work keep a recovering service overloaded, and retry budgets help
Orders stayed at 0% success for 70 seconds after the dependency recovered (title)

brief.reader: Platform or SRE engineer running services on Kubernetes that call each other over HTTP, watching them in Splunk Observability Cloud
brief.decision: How their service-to-service retries should behave so a short slowdown in one dependency ends when the dependency recovers, instead of turning into a longer outage
brief.question: Why does my service stay down after the dependency is healthy again, and how do I see a retry storm in Splunk APM?
brief.takeaway: After a 20-second slowdown, watch what instant retries do to a dependency that is already healthy again, measured three times per policy: failed orders, recovery to 95% success, calls per order, and how much of inventory's work started after the caller had already given up. Then the same with exponential backoff, full jitter and a retry budget, credited together as one fix, and the same windows in Splunk APM.
brief.adds: The AWS Builders' Library and Google SRE book explain retry storms and backoff with jitter in prose. This post runs both policies against the same slowdown on EKS, counts failed orders and calls per order second by second, and reads the same windows back from Splunk Observability Cloud, with the service map from Splunk APM.
brief.open_question: After a 20-second slowdown in inventory, with orders arriving at a steady 40 a second, in three alternating runs per policy: how many orders fail in the next 70 seconds, does success return to 95% within that window and how fast, how many inventory calls does each order make, and what share of inventory's work starts after the caller's timeout has passed, with instant retries compared with backoff, full jitter and a 10% retry budget together?
tradeoffs: The budget policy combines backoff, full jitter and a retry budget; the lab credits the combination, not any one part
A retry budget means some orders fail without a retry while the budget is spent; the lab counts those skipped retries
Backoff adds latency to the orders that retry; the lab reports p50 and p99 latency of successful orders before and after the slowdown in every run
The slowdown is simulated (2 s per request for 20 s), with one load level, one timeout (500 ms) and one dependency
The backlog of abandoned requests still drains after the slowdown; server-side load shedding is not tested

measurements.what: percent of orders that succeeded in the 20 seconds before the slowdown, the positive control that each run started healthy: naive-1, naive-2, naive-3, budget-1, budget-2, budget-3
orders that failed in the 70 seconds after the 20-second slowdown ended, for each of the six runs
per run: recovered (1 if orders got back to at least 95% success for 5 seconds in a row within 70 seconds of the slowdown ending, else 0) and, for runs that recovered, seconds until they did

per run, in the 70 seconds after the slowdown: inventory calls per order, failed calls that timed out, failed calls refused or reset (kept apart from timeouts so a full listen queue would show), and for budget runs the retries the budget skipped

percent of the requests inventory handled in the 70 seconds after the slowdown that it started after the caller's 500 ms timeout had passed, from the X-Caller-Deadline header, for each of the six runs
the largest number of requests inventory had accepted but not yet started (waiting for one of its 4 threads), sampled every second in the 70 seconds after the slowdown, for each of the six runs

p50 and p99 latency of successful orders in the 20 seconds before the slowdown and in the 70 seconds after it, for each run, with n printed beside each; a run with no successful orders after the slowdown reports null there

in the 70 seconds after the slowdown, per run: average and busiest-second CPU cores of the inventory and orders containers from their cgroups, and the node's busiest-second CPU percent from /proc/stat, to show whether a busy node rather than the retries held inventory back

percent of orders requests that Splunk Observability Cloud counted as 503s in the window after the slowdown, on 10-second boundaries, from the services' OpenTelemetry HTTP server metric: naive-2, budget-2

percent difference between Splunk Observability Cloud's orders request count (OpenTelemetry HTTP server metric, orders route) and the load's own count for the same window, on 10-second boundaries; orders arrive at a steady 40 a second, so bucket edges can't move it (inventory's comparison is printed too, but its rate changes fast after the slowdown): naive-2, budget-2
